hints: Start by recalling what makes any nitrogen compound basic, think about what the lone pair on N must do to a proton.
Compare the environment of the N lone pair in an amide with that in a simple amine, consider where else the electrons could go.
Compare propylamine with ammonia, think about how a propyl alkyl group pushes electron density toward or away from N.
Put the three compounds in order by asking which lone pair is least available and which is most available for bonding to $H^+$.
walkthrough:
Picture basicity as lone pair availability**
Think of a base as a lone pair looking for a proton. All three compounds have a nitrogen with a lone pair, so the strongest base will be the one whose lone pair is most ready to form a new $N-H^+$ bond. Availability is everything.

See why the amide is the weakest**
In $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$ the nitrogen sits right next to a $C=O$. The lone pair on N overlaps with the pi system and is delocalised over the $N-C-O$ unit toward electronegative oxygen. Because those electrons are already busy in resonance, they are much less free to pick up $H^+$. That makes propanamide a very weak base.

See why the alkyl amine is the strongest**
In $CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$ the nitrogen is attached to a propyl group. Alkyl groups push electron density toward N by the positive inductive effect. That increases electron density on N, makes the lone pair more negative and more eager to bond to $H^+$. So propylamine is more basic than ammonia, $NH_3$, which has no such donating group.

Assemble the order**
Least available lone pair is in the delocalised amide, intermediate is ammonia, most available is the alkyl enriched amine. Hence: $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$ < $NH_3$ < $CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$ from weakest to strongest base.

Final answer: propanamide < ammonia < propylamine, weakest to strongest base.
Basicity depends on availability of the lone pair / p orbital on N to accept / donate to $H^+$.
In propanamide the N lone pair is delocalised into the $C=O$ / over the $N-C-O$ group, so less available.
In propylamine the propyl / alkyl group is electron donating by positive inductive effect, so lone pair more available.

hints: For K, work backwards from $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$ formed with $NH_3$, recall which carboxylic acid derivative reacts with ammonia to give an amide.
For L, look at $CH_3CH_2Br$ with $KCN$ in ethanol, recall what happens to the carbon chain length when $CN^-$ acts as a nucleophile.
For M, notice both an amide and a nitrile are converted to the same primary amine, recall the strong reducing agent that can do both reductions.
walkthrough:
Deduce K from amide formation**
You see K + $NH_3$ gives $CH_3CH_2CONH_2$. Amides are made very readily from acyl chlorides plus ammonia. So K must supply the $CH_3CH_2CO$ fragment with a good leaving group, that is $CH_3CH_2COCl$, propanoyl chloride.

Deduce L from chain extension**
$CH_3CH_2Br$ + $KCN$ in ethanol is classic nucleophilic substitution by $CN^-$. Bromide leaves and $CN$ adds, giving $CH_3CH_2CN$. Notice the chain grows by one carbon, from a 2 carbon bromoalkane to a 3 carbon nitrile, propanenitrile.

Identify the common reducing agent M**
Both routes finish at $CH_3CH_2CH_2NH_2$. Reduction of a nitrile $R-CN$ and reduction of an amide $R-CONH_2$ to a primary amine both need a powerful hydride donor. $LiAlH_4$ does both, and catalytic hydrogenation with $H_2$ / Ni also reduces nitriles. So M is $LiAlH_4$ or $H_2$ / Ni.

Final answer: K = $CH_3CH_2COCl$ / propanoyl chloride
L = $CH_3CH_2CN$ / propanenitrile
M = $LiAlH_4$ or $H_2$ / Ni

hints: Locate the hydrolysable bonds in N, count how many amide $CONH$ linkages are present and ignore the $CH_3O$ ether.
Recall that hot concentrated $HCl$ cleaves each amide into a carboxylic acid plus an amine, which under excess acid becomes protonated.
Split the molecule at the two $C-N$ amide bonds and write the three carbon skeletons: benzyl fragment, central amino acid fragment, acetyl fragment.
At pH 4 think about which groups stay protonated, amines as $-NH_3^+$ and acids as $-COOH$, not $-COO^-$.
walkthrough:
Spot the two amides to cut**
Draw N out: $C_6H_5CH_2-NH-CO-CH(NHCOCH_3)-CH_2OCH_3$. There are two amide links: one linking benzyl amine to the central acid, and one acetyl amide on the central nitrogen. The $CH_3-O-$ ether is told to ignore, it survives.

Hydrolyse each amide in concentrated acid**
Acid hydrolysis adds water across each $CO-NH$ bond to give $COOH$ + $H_2N$. So cutting both gives three pieces: $C_6H_5CH_2NH_2$, $HOOC-CH(NH_2)-CH_2OCH_3$, and $CH_3COOH$. In excess concentrated $HCl$ the amines are immediately protonated.

Apply the pH 4 isolation condition**
At pH 4, which is acidic, amines exist as $-NH_3^+$ and carboxylic acids exist mainly as neutral $-COOH$ rather than $-COO^-$. So write $C_6H_5CH_2NH_3^+$, $HOOC-CH(NH_3^+)-CH_2-O-CH_3$, and neutral $CH_3COOH$.

Check atom balance**
You started with two nitrogens and two carbonyl carbons in amides. You finish with two $-NH_3^+$ groups and two $-COOH$ groups plus the unchanged ether. That confirms complete hydrolysis to three organic products.

Final answer: Products at pH 4 are:
$C_6H_5CH_2NH_3^+$ / protonated benzylamine
$HOOC-CH(NH_3^+)-CH_2-O-CH_3$ / protonated amino acid with $COOH$ and $NH_3^+$
$CH_3COOH$ / ethanoic acid
All $-NH_2$ present as $-NH_3^+$ and all $-COOH$ present as $COOH$.

hints: Count O atoms in $NO_2$ that must be removed as water and work out how many $[H]$ are needed to make $NH_2$ plus $H_2O$.
walkthrough:
Balance the nitro to amine reduction**
Converting $-NO_2$ to $-NH_2$ needs to strip two oxygens as $2H_2O$ and add two hydrogens to N. That requires six atoms of hydrogen from the reducing agent: $$C_7H_7NO_2 + 6[H] \rightarrow C_7H_7NH_2 + 2H_2O$$ Check H: 7+6 = 9 on left, 9+4 = 13? Wait count carefully: right has $C_7H_7NH_2$ which is $C_7H_9N$ plus $2H_2O$ which is $H_4$, total $H_{13}$, left has $H_7 + H_6 = H_{13}$. Balanced.

hints: For step 1, recall the classic reagents that reduce an aromatic $NO_2$ to $NH_2$ using a metal plus concentrated acid with heat.
For step 2, see $NH_2$ becoming $N(CH_3)_2$, think about which methyl halide can methylate the amine by nucleophilic substitution.
For step 2 type, decide what class of reaction occurs when an amine lone pair attacks a haloalkane.
For step 3, see a ring $CH_3$ becoming $COOH$ while $N(CH_3)_2$ survives, recall the vigorous oxidant for side chain oxidation.
For step 3 type, name the reaction class when an alkyl side chain gains oxygen to form a carboxylic acid.
For step 4, see $COOH$ plus an alcohol forming an ester P, identify the branched primary alcohol and the acid catalyst needed for condensation.
walkthrough:
Step 1, reduce the nitro group**
1-methyl-4-nitrobenzene to 1-methyl-4-aminobenzene is reduction. The standard Paper 4 reagent is tin and concentrated $HCl$ with heat, followed by alkali work up. So write $Sn$ + conc. $HCl$, heat, type = reduction.

Step 2, dimethylate the amine**
$Ar-NH_2$ to $Ar-N(CH_3)_2$ adds two methyl groups to nitrogen. The amine acts as a nucleophile attacking a methyl halide such as $CH_3Br$ (or $CH_3Cl$, $CH_3I$) in ethanol, displacing halide. Excess halide gives the tertiary amine. Type = nucleophilic substitution.

Step 3, oxidise the ring methyl to acid**
Now the $CH_3$ attached to the ring becomes $COOH$ while the $N(CH_3)_2$ group stays intact. This is vigorous side chain oxidation, needing hot alkaline or acidified $KMnO_4$, written as hot $MnO_4^-$. Type = oxidation.

Step 4, make the ester P by condensation**
Carboxylic acid to ester with the branched alcohol shown in P. The alcohol fragment is $-OCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)_2$, so the alcohol is $HOCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)_2$, 3-methylbutan-1-ol, with conc. $H_2SO_4$ catalyst and heat. Carboxylic acid + alcohol to ester + water is condensation (esterification).

Final answer: Step 1: $Sn$ and conc. $HCl$ (+ heat), reduction
Step 2: $CH_3Br$ / $CH_3Cl$ / $CH_3I$ (in ethanol), (nucleophilic) substitution
Step 3: hot $MnO_4^-$ / $KMnO_4$, oxidation
Step 4: $HOCH_2CH_2CH(CH_3)_2$ / 3-methylbutan-1-ol (+ conc. $H_2SO_4$), condensation
